facts.fact: Pieter Bleeker described the species in 1854, originally in the genus Syngnathus.
The original description appeared in Verhandelingen van het Bataviaasch Genootschap van Kunsten en Wetenschappen, vol. 25.
The type locality is Jakarta, on Java, Indonesia. The syntypes are held at RMNH.
It is now placed in Microphis (subfamily Nerophinae) and was formerly placed in Coelonotus.
The genus name Microphis comes from the Greek for 'small' and 'serpent'.
It has an eel-like body, no dorsal spines, 53–63 dorsal soft rays and 27–33 tail rings.
It is assessed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List (2016).
It is a close relative of seahorses, in the same family.
The body is very long, thin and almost cylindrical, with a long tubular snout.
A tiny, fast-beating dorsal fin provides almost all of its movement.
It is recorded from Indonesia, Japan, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands and New Caledonia.
Its range covers the western Pacific, from Indonesia east to the Philippines and the Mariana Islands, north to Kagoshima Prefecture in southern Japan and south to New Caledonia.
It occurs in clear streams of Australia's Wet Tropics World Heritage Area.
It is widespread in parts of Southeast Asia and the western Pacific.
It lives in fresh and brackish water: streams, rivers and estuaries, down to about 5 m depth.
It is amphidromous, linking freshwater streams with the sea during its life cycle.
It lives in the lower-mid course of short, steep coastal streams, where it is associated with pebble fields.
Adults live in slow-moving rivers and streams, but its life cycle is tied to coastal waters.
It is rarely seen in the aquarium hobby.
It is offered for sale in the hobby through The Wet Spot Tropical Fish.
It is not a fish for beginners and suits keepers who can culture live food.
In the Australian Wet Tropics, people stacking stones, building rock dams and skimming stones disturb its habitat.
Researchers recommend a 'leave no trace' approach in its streams to protect it.
It is of no fisheries interest.
A species tank or a very calm setup gives the best long-term results.
Temperatures of 21–24 °C are recommended.
A neutral to slightly acidic pH is recommended.
Strong current should be avoided, but gentle circulation and good oxygenation are needed.
Stable water matters more than exact parameters, because sudden swings cause problems.
It prefers a dim, densely planted, mature tank with roots, driftwood and leaf litter, like a slow forest stream.
In the wild it feeds on microscopic benthic invertebrates.
It hunts tiny live prey such as copepods, cyclops, insect larvae and small shrimp, using a fast suction strike.
It usually ignores flakes and pellets. Newly imported fish may not recognise frozen food.
Live food is essential at first. Some individuals can later be weaned onto frozen cyclops or Artemia nauplii.
It moves slowly and deliberately, hovering to search leaves, roots and wood for food.
It competes poorly for food, so active tank mates such as tetras, rainbowfish and corydoras outcompete it.
Males have a brood pouch under the tail.
In the wild it is ovoviviparous, with the male carrying the eggs in a brood pouch under the tail.
In the wild, males may be brooding at 11.25 cm SL, and length at maturity is about 11 cm.

After a mating dance, the female places her eggs in the male's brood pouch, he fertilises them, and fully formed young later emerge. The video does not say whether this describes wild or aquarium breeding.
